Arnaud Ducrot Address: UNIHAVRE, LMAH, FR-CNRS-3335, ISCN, Normandie University, 76600 Le Havre, France Email address: arnaud.ducrot@univ-lehavre.fr , Thomas Giletti Address: Institut Elie Cartan Lorraine, UMR 7502, University of Lorraine, 54506 Vandoeuvre-lès-Nancy, France Email address: thomas.giletti@univ-lorraine.fr , Jong-Shenq Guo Address: Department of Mathematics, Tamkang University, Tamsui, New Taipei City 251301, Taiwan Email address: jsguo @ mail.tku.edu.tw and Masahiko Shimojo Address: Department of Applied Mathematics, Okayama University of Science, Okayama 700-0005, Japan Email address: shimojo@xmath.ous.ac.jp
Abstract.

This paper investigates the large time behaviour of a three species reaction-diffusion system, modelling the spatial invasion of two predators feeding on a single prey species. In addition to the competition for food, the two predators exhibit competitive interactions and under some parameter conditions (μ>0\mu>0), they can also be considered as two mutants. When mutations occur in the predator populations, the spatial spread of invasion takes place at a definite speed, identical for both mutants. When the two predators are not coupled through mutation, the spreading behaviour exhibits a more complex propagating pattern, including multiple layers with different speeds. In addition, some parameter conditions reveal situations where a nonlocal pulling phenomenon occurs and in particular where the spreading speed is not linearly determined.

1. Introduction

In this work we study the large time behaviour for the following three-species predator-prey system

(1.1) ut=d1​ux​x+u​F​(u,v,w)+μ⁡(v−u)in(0,+∞)×ℝ,\displaystyle u_{t}=d_{1}u_{xx}+uF(u,v,w)+\mu(v-u)\quad\mbox{in}\quad(0,+\infty)\times\mathbb{R},
(1.2) vt=d2​vx​x+v​G​(u,v,w)+μ⁡(u−v)in(0,+∞)×ℝ,\displaystyle v_{t}=d_{2}v_{xx}+vG(u,v,w)+\mu(u-v)\quad\mbox{in}\quad(0,+\infty)\times\mathbb{R},
(1.3) wt=d3​wx​x+w​H​(u,v,w)in(0,+∞)×ℝ,\displaystyle w_{t}=d_{3}w_{xx}+wH(u,v,w)\quad\mbox{in}\quad(0,+\infty)\times\mathbb{R},

wherein the functions FF, GG and HH are respectively given by

F⁡(u,v,w):=r1​(−1−u−k​v+a​w),\displaystyle F(u,v,w):=r_{1}(-1-u-kv+aw),
G⁡(u,v,w):=r2​(−1−h​u−v+a​w),\displaystyle G(u,v,w):=r_{2}(-1-hu-v+aw),
H⁡(u,v,w):=r3​(1−b​u−b​v−w).\displaystyle H(u,v,w):=r_{3}(1-bu-bv-w).

Here u=u⁡(t,x)u=u(t,x) and v=v⁡(t,x)v=v(t,x) denote the densities of two predators and w=w⁡(t,x)w=w(t,x) corresponds to the density of the single prey. The parameters did_{i}, rir_{i} in system (1.1)-(1.3) are all positive and respectively stand for the motility and per capita growth rate of each species. The parameters h>0h>0 and k>0k>0 represent the competition between the two predators while a>0a>0 and b>0b>0 describe the predator-prey interactions. The parameter μ\mu is assumed to be nonnegative.

When μ>0\mu>0 it stands as a mutation rate between species uu and vv, so that the two predators are mutant species. Therefore, one should distinguish the case μ=0\mu=0, where uu and vv can be understood as completely distinct species which are competing for the same prey, from the case μ>0\mu>0 where uu and vv are the densities of two mutants of the same predator species, both feeding on the same prey. Both situations also lead to very different large time behaviours of the solutions. We shall refer to the former as the ‘two competitors’ case, and to the latter as the ‘two mutants’ case.

To perform our study of system (1.1)-(1.3), we impose the following parameter conditions

(1.4) a>1,0<h,k<1,0<b<12​(a−1),0≤μ≤a−12​min⁡{r1,r2}.a>1,\quad 0<h,k<1,\quad 0<b<\frac{1}{2(a-1)},\quad 0\leq\mu\leq\frac{a-1}{2}\min\{r_{1},r_{2}\}.

Condition (1.4) shall be assumed throughout this paper, and as we shall see below it typically allows the possibility of co-existence of all three species.

The main goal of this paper is to study the asymptotic spreading speed(s) of the two invading predators into a prey population uniformly close to its carrying capacity. For this purpose, we typically investigate the Cauchy problem for (1.1)-(1.3) with the initial condition

(1.5) u⁡(0,x)=u0​(x),v⁡(0,x)=v0​(x),w⁡(0,x)=w0​(x),x∈ℝ,u(0,x)=u_{0}(x),\quad v(0,x)=v_{0}(x),\quad w(0,x)=w_{0}(x),\quad x\in\mathbb{R},

where initial data u0,v0,w0u_{0},v_{0},w_{0} are uniformly continuous functions defined on ℝ\mathbb{R}, both u0u_{0} and v0v_{0} have nontrivial compact supports, and

(1.6) 0≤u0,v0≤a−1,β≤w0≤1​ on ℝ.0\leq u_{0},\;v_{0}\leq a-1,\quad\beta\leq w_{0}\leq 1\;\mbox{ on $\mathbb{R}$.}

Hereafter, we set β:=1−2​b​(a−1)>0\beta:=1-2b(a-1)>0 in which the positivity follows from the third condition in (1.4). Note that by the classical theory of reaction-diffusion systems there is a unique global (in time) solution (u,v,w)(u,v,w) of the Cauchy problem for system (1.1)-(1.3) with initial condition (1.5) for any uniformly continuous initial data (u0,v0,w0)(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0}) satisfying (1.6).

The description of spatial propagation for diffusive predator-prey systems has a long history. In particular, traveling wave solutions have been exhibited in a wide range of predator-prey systems. For the systems with exactly one prey and one predator, we refer in particular to the pioneering works [9, 10]. We also refer to [18, 16, 20] and the references cited therein for more results about traveling waves in such a context. Recently, more attention is paid to the existence of traveling waves of some three species predator-prey systems. For this, we refer the reader to, e.g., [2, 17] for a diffusive system involving two preys and one predator, and [15, 19] for a system with two predators and one prey.

While some stability results were obtained in [11], it is only recently that a more exhaustive study of the spreading properties of solutions of the Cauchy problem has been performed for systems with one prey and one predator [5, 6, 8, 22]. This naturally raises the question of propagation phenomena in more realistic systems involving a larger number of interacting species. Let us mention in particular that the spreading speed of the predator for a three-species predator-prey system with a single predator and two preys was studied by Wu [23].

As far as mutant systems are considered, we refer to Griette and Raoul [14] for a study of traveling wave solutions. We also refer to Girardin [12] for a result on the asymptotic spreading speed of solutions of the Cauchy problem and to Morris et al [21] for discussion about the linear determinacy of the spreading speed. However, those earlier works were concerned with systems coupling mutations and competitive interactions between the mutants. As far as we know, our work is the first to investigate the spreading properties in a situation involving both mutations and prey-predator interactions.

One important difficulty to be overcome in our analysis of the spreading properties for system (1.1)-(1.3) with (1.5) is the lack of comparison principle. In addition, as described below, the ‘two-competitors’ system admits different semi-trivial equilibria that generate complex propagating behaviour, including the development of multiple propagating layers with different speeds. These difficulties are overcome by using refined dynamical system arguments and by carefully investigating suitable omega-limit solutions in various and adapted moving frames.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. First, Section 2 is devoted to the description of the main results obtained in this paper. This comes after introducing some notation to be used throughout this paper. Then we start in Section 3 with some preliminaries. These preliminaries include a priori estimates on solutions and the computation of the principal eigenvalues of some linearized systems which shall arise in the proof of our main results. Moreover, we establish some persistence result, Lemma 3.2, which shall be a key ingredient in our arguments, in the spirit of [6]. Then, in Section 4, we show by a Lyapunov like argument that, in the ‘two competitors case’, bounded entire in time solutions which are bounded from below by some positive constants must be identical to a steady state.

The later sections are directly concerned with the proofs of our main results described in Section 2. Section 5 mostly deals with the ‘two mutants’ case and some general upper bounds on the spreading speeds, both for the ‘two mutants’ and ‘two competitors’ cases. Next, in Section 6 we establish some of the lower bounds on the speeds in the ‘two competitors’ case. Then in Section 7 we deal with the case when both predator species have the same speed and diffusivity. Finally, in Section 8, we first derive the definite spreading speed of the faster predator in the ‘two competitors’ case. Then we exhibit a ‘nonlocal pulling’ phenomenon for the slower predator. This leaves a question on the definite spreading speed of the slower predator to be open.

2. Main results

In this section, we state the main results that shall be proved and discussed in this paper. We start by introducing some notation and important quantities before going to the description of our main spreading results.

2.1. Some notation

2.1.1. Constant equilibria

Let us first look at the underlying ODE system. It is clear that (0,0,0)(0,0,0) and (0,0,1)(0,0,1) (the predator-free state) are two trivial equilibria for system (1.1)-(1.3); both are linearly unstable. For other steady states, we consider separately the ‘two competitors’ and the ‘two mutants’ cases. In both cases, we shall find that the three components ultimately persist in the large time behaviour of solutions of (1.1)-(1.3). Furthermore, in the first case, the solution converges to the unique co-existence steady state which we compute below.

Two competitors case μ=0\mu=0: It is easy to check that, when a>1a>1, (0,p~,q~)(0,\tilde{p},\tilde{q}) and (p~,0,q~)(\tilde{p},0,\tilde{q}) are two semi-trivial steady states of system (1.1)-(1.3), where

(2.1) p~=a−11+a​b,q~=b+11+a​b.\tilde{p}=\frac{a-1}{1+ab},\quad\tilde{q}=\frac{b+1}{1+ab}.

Moreover, under condition (1.4) there is a unique positive co-existence state (u∗,v∗,w∗)(u^{*},v^{*},w^{*}), where

(2.2) u∗:=1−k1−h​k(aw∗−1),v∗:=1−h1−h​k(aw∗−1),w∗:=(1−h​k)+b⁡(2−h−k)(1−h​k)+a​b​(2−h−k).\begin{split}&u^{*}:=\frac{1-k}{1-hk}(aw^{*}-1),\quad v^{*}:=\frac{1-h}{1-hk}(aw^{*}-1),\\ &w^{*}:=\frac{(1-hk)+b(2-h-k)}{(1-hk)+ab(2-h-k)}.\end{split}

Note that one has

F⁡(0,p~,q~)=r11+a​b​(a−1)​(1−k)>0,G⁡(p~,0,q~)=r21+a​b​(a−1)​(1−h)>0.\displaystyle F(0,\tilde{p},\tilde{q})=\frac{r_{1}}{1+ab}(a-1)(1-k)>0,\quad G(\tilde{p},0,\tilde{q})=\frac{r_{2}}{1+ab}(a-1)(1-h)>0.

This means that the semi-trivial steady states are unstable with respect to the underlying kinetic ODE system.

Two mutants case μ>0\mu>0: In this case, because of the coupling between the two mutants it is clear that there cannot exist a semi-trivial steady state of system (1.1)-(1.3). However, as in the case μ=0\mu=0, there typically exists a unique positive co-existence steady state (uμ∗,vμ∗,wμ∗)(u^{*}_{\mu},v^{*}_{\mu},w^{*}_{\mu}). This can be checked proceeding as in [14] provided that μ\mu is small enough. Note that, as discussed in [3], the mutation rate μ\mu is typically small for relevant biological situations. Since a more detailed analysis of the equilibria is not necessary to our purpose, we omit the details.

2.1.2. Linear speeds

We shall take an interest in the invasion of predators on the predator-free state. Consider the linearization of (1.1) and (1.2) around the predator-free state (0,0,1)(0,0,1), and write it in matrix form as

(utvt)=(d1​ux​xd2​vx​x)+M⁡[μ]×(uv),\left(\begin{array}[]{c}u_{t}\\ v_{t}\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}d_{1}u_{xx}\\ d_{2}v_{xx}\end{array}\right)+M[\mu]\times\left(\begin{array}[]{c}u\\ v\end{array}\right),

where

M⁡[μ]:=[r1​(a−1)−μμμr2​(a−1)−μ].M[\mu]:=\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}r_{1}(a-1)-\mu&\mu\\ \mu&r_{2}(a-1)-\mu\end{array}\right].

In the case when μ>0\mu>0, the components uu and vv are mutants of the same species and therefore they should spread simultaneously. By analogy with the scalar equation, one may want to look for an ansatz of the type

(u,v)=(p,q)​e−γ⁡(x−c​t),p,q,γ>0,c∈ℝ.(u,v)=(p,q)e^{-\gamma(x-ct)},\quad p,q,\gamma>0,\;c\in\mathbb{R}.

Putting this in the above equation, one finds that (p,q)(p,q) and γ\gamma must solve

M⁡[μ,γ]×(pq)=c​γ​(pq),M[\mu,\gamma]\times\left(\begin{array}[]{c}p\\ q\end{array}\right)=c\gamma\left(\begin{array}[]{c}p\\ q\end{array}\right),

where

(2.3) M⁡[μ,γ]:=[d1​γ2+r1​(a−1)−μμμd2​γ2+r2​(a−1)−μ].M[\mu,\gamma]:=\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}d_{1}\gamma^{2}+r_{1}(a-1)-\mu&\mu\\ \mu&d_{2}\gamma^{2}+r_{2}(a-1)-\mu\end{array}\right].

This leads us to introduce

(2.4) cμ∗:=minγ>0⁡Λ⁡[μ,γ]γ>0,c_{\mu}^{*}:=\min_{\gamma>0}\frac{\Lambda[\mu,\gamma]}{\gamma}>0,

such that an ansatz of the above type solves the linearized system around the predator-free state if and only if c≥cμ∗c\geq c_{\mu}^{*}. Here Λ⁡[μ,γ]\Lambda[\mu,\gamma] denotes the unique principal eigenvalue of M⁡[μ,γ]M[\mu,\gamma], which exists by applying Perron-Frobenius theorem. We point out that the existence and positivity of cμ∗c_{\mu}^{*} are ensured by the fact that Λ⁡[μ,0]>0\Lambda[\mu,0]>0 (recall that 2​μ≤(a−1)​min⁡{r1,r2}2\mu\leq(a-1)\min\{r_{1},r_{2}\}) and γ↦Λ⁡[μ,γ]\gamma\mapsto\Lambda[\mu,\gamma] is convex.

In the case when μ=0\mu=0, the functions uu and vv are population densities of distinct species which may spread with different speeds. This can be seen in the fact that the matrix M⁡[0]M[0] is no longer irreducible; one can then find semi-trivial ansatzes

(u,v)=(p,0)e−γ⁡(x−c​t),(u,v)=(0,q)e−γ⁡(x−c​t),p,q>0.(u,v)=(p,0)e^{-\gamma(x-ct)},\quad(u,v)=(0,q)e^{-\gamma(x-ct)},\quad p,q>0.

These exist if, respectively, c≥cu∗c\geq c^{*}_{u} and c≥cv∗c\geq c^{*}_{v}. Those speeds are explicitly defined as

(2.5) cu∗:=2​d1​r1​(a−1),cv∗:=2​d2​r2​(a−1).c_{u}^{*}:=2\sqrt{d_{1}r_{1}(a-1)},\quad c_{v}^{*}:=2\sqrt{d_{2}r_{2}(a-1)}.

One may check that cμ∗c^{*}_{\mu} converges to max⁡{cu∗,cv∗}\max\{c_{u}^{*},c_{v}^{*}\} as μ→0\mu\to 0. Without loss of generality, we may assume that d1​r1≥d2​r2d_{1}r_{1}\geq d_{2}r_{2}. Hence throughout this paper we always assume that

cu∗≥cv∗.c_{u}^{*}\geq c_{v}^{*}.

In the case when μ=0\mu=0, it is then expected that the component uu shall spread with speed cu∗c_{u}^{*}, and the component vv at some slower speed. However, this means that vv may no longer invade in the predator-free state. This leads us to introduce

(2.6) cu∗⁣∗:=2​d1​r11+a​b​(a−1)​(1−k)=cu∗​1−k1+a​b,cv∗⁣∗:=2​1−h1+a​b​d2​r2​(a−1)=cv∗​1−h1+a​b.\begin{split}&c_{u}^{**}:=2\sqrt{\frac{d_{1}r_{1}}{1+ab}(a-1)(1-k)}=c_{u}^{*}\sqrt{\frac{1-k}{1+ab}},\\ &c_{v}^{**}:=2\sqrt{\frac{1-h}{1+ab}d_{2}r_{2}(a-1)}=c_{v}^{*}\sqrt{\frac{1-h}{1+ab}}.\end{split}

Note that cv∗⁣∗<cv∗c_{v}^{**}<c_{v}^{*} and cv∗⁣∗c_{v}^{**} is the spreading speed of solutions of

vt=d2​vx​x+r2​v​(−1−h​p~+a​q~),\displaystyle v_{t}=d_{2}v_{xx}+r_{2}v(-1-h\tilde{p}+a\tilde{q}),

i.e., the linear invasion speed into the semi-trivial steady state (when μ=0\mu=0) where uu and ww coexist.

2.2. Our main results

We are now in a position to describe the spreading speed of solutions. In the sequel, we let (u,v,w)(u,v,w) be a solution of the Cauchy problem for system (1.1)-(1.3) with the initial condition (1.5), under the assumption (1.6).

Our first theorem deals with the ‘two mutants’ case μ>0\mu>0 where we can describe accurately the spreading speed of the solution:

Theorem 2.1.

Assume that (1.4) holds and that in addition μ>0\mu>0. Let (u0,v0)(u_{0},v_{0}) be nontrivial and compactly supported such that 0≤u0,v0≤a−10\leq u_{0},v_{0}\leq a-1, and β≤w0≤1\beta\leq w_{0}\leq 1. Recall also that cμ∗c^{*}_{\mu} is defined by (2.4). Then the solution (u,v,w)(u,v,w) enjoys the following spreading behaviour:

  • (i)

    for any c>cμ∗c>c^{*}_{\mu},

    limt→+∞sup|x|≥c​t{|u⁡(t,x)|+|v⁡(t,x)|+|1−w⁡(t,x)|}=0;\lim_{t\to+\infty}\sup_{|x|\geq ct}\{|u(t,x)|+|v(t,x)|+|1-w(t,x)|\}=0;
  • (ii)

    for any c∈[0,cμ∗)c\in[0,c^{*}_{\mu}),

    lim inft→+∞inf|x|≤c​tmin⁡{u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x),1−w⁡(t,x)}>0.\liminf_{t\to+\infty}\inf_{|x|\leq ct}\min\{u(t,x),v(t,x),1-w(t,x)\}>0.

The above result shows that both predator mutants spread with the same asymptotic speed. However, the question of the convergence to a steady state in the wake of the propagation remains open.

Let us now turn to the ‘two competitors’ case μ=0\mu=0. This situation turns out to be more complicated, because unlike in the ‘two mutants’ case the subsystem (1.1) and (1.2) with constant ww has no cooperative structure in the neighborhood of (0,0)(0,0). Moreover, both competitors may spread with different spreading speeds, so that ultimately one may observe three zones: ahead of the propagation in the predator-free state, after the propagation of the first predator but before arrival of the second, and finally a co-existence state where all three species persist.

The next theorem provides some estimates on the spreading speeds of both species.

Theorem 2.2.

Assume that (1.4) holds and that in addition μ=0\mu=0. Let both u0u_{0} and v0v_{0} be nontrivial and compactly supported such that 0≤u0,v0≤a−10\leq u_{0},v_{0}\leq a-1, and β≤w0≤1\beta\leq w_{0}\leq 1. Recall also that cu∗c_{u}^{*} and cv∗c_{v}^{*} are defined in (2.5). Then the solution (u,v,w)(u,v,w) satisfies, for any c>cu∗c>c_{u}^{*},

limt→+∞sup|x|≥c​tu⁡(t,x)=0,\displaystyle\lim_{t\to+\infty}\sup_{|x|\geq ct}u(t,x)=0,

and, for any c>cv∗c>c_{v}^{*},

limt→+∞sup|x|≥c​tv⁡(t,x)=0.\displaystyle\lim_{t\to+\infty}\sup_{|x|\geq ct}v(t,x)=0.

Moreover, for any c>max⁡{cu∗,cv∗}c>\max\{c_{u}^{*},c_{v}^{*}\},

limt→+∞sup|x|≥c​t|1−w⁡(t,x)|=0.\displaystyle\lim_{t\to+\infty}\sup_{|x|\geq ct}|1-w(t,x)|=0.

In particular, this result states that uu and vv spread at most, respectively, with speeds cu∗c_{u}^{*} and cv∗c_{v}^{*}. Now the question is whether cu∗c_{u}^{*} and cv∗c_{v}^{*} are indeed the spreading speed of uu and vv. To answer this point, we consider separately the cases when cv∗=cu∗c_{v}^{*}=c_{u}^{*} and cv∗<cu∗c_{v}^{*}<c_{u}^{*}.

Assume that (1.4) holds and that in addition μ=0\mu=0 and cv∗=cu∗c_{v}^{*}=c_{u}^{*}. Theorem 2.4.

Under the same assumptions as Theorem 2.2, suppose also that w0≡1w_{0}\equiv 1, d1=d2d_{1}=d_{2} and r1=r2r_{1}=r_{2}, so that in particular cu∗=cv∗c_{u}^{*}=c_{v}^{*}. Then, for any c∈[0,cu∗)c\in[0,c_{u}^{*}),

lim inft→+∞inf|x|≤c​tu⁡(t,x)>0,\liminf_{t\to+\infty}\inf_{|x|\leq ct}u(t,x)>0,

if u0≥κ​v0u_{0}\geq\kappa v_{0}; while, for any c∈[0,cv∗)c\in[0,c_{v}^{*}), if u0≤κ​v0u_{0}\leq\kappa v_{0} we have

lim inft→+∞inf|x|≤c​tv⁡(t,x)>0.\liminf_{t\to+\infty}\inf_{|x|\leq ct}v(t,x)>0.

In each case, we also have

lim supt→+∞sup|x|≤c​tw⁡(t,x)<1.\limsup_{t\to+\infty}\sup_{|x|\leq ct}w(t,x)<1.

We now turn to the case when cv∗<cu∗c_{v}^{*}<c_{u}^{*}, where the following result answers positively that cu∗c_{u}^{*} is indeed the spreading speed of uu.

Theorem 2.5.

Assume that (1.4) holds and that in addition μ=0\mu=0 and cv∗<cu∗c_{v}^{*}<c_{u}^{*}. Let both u0u_{0} and v0v_{0} be nontrivial and compactly supported such that 0≤u0,v0≤a−10\leq u_{0},v_{0}\leq a-1, and β≤w0≤1\beta\leq w_{0}\leq 1. Then the solution (u,v,w)(u,v,w) enjoys the following spreading behaviour:

  • (i)

    for each c∈[0,cu∗)c\in[0,c_{u}^{*}), one has

    lim inft→+∞inf|x|≤c​tu⁡(t,x)>0;\liminf_{t\to+\infty}\inf_{|x|\leq ct}u(t,x)>0;
  • (ii)

    for any cv∗<c1<c2<cu∗c_{v}^{*}<c_{1}<c_{2}<c_{u}^{*},

    limt→+∞supc1​t≤|x|≤c2​t‖(u,v,w)​(t,x)−(p~,0,q~)‖=0,\lim_{t\to+\infty}\sup_{c_{1}t\leq|x|\leq c_{2}t}\left\|(u,v,w)(t,x)-\left(\tilde{p},0,\tilde{q}\right)\right\|=0,

    wherein (p~,0,q~)\left(\tilde{p},0,\tilde{q}\right) is the constant equilibrium defined in (2.1);

  • (iii)

    finally, for each 0<c<cv∗⁣∗0<c<c_{v}^{**},

    limt→+∞sup|x|≤c​t‖(u,v,w)​(t,x)−(u∗,v∗,w∗)‖=0.\lim_{t\to+\infty}\sup_{|x|\leq ct}\left\|(u,v,w)(t,x)-(u^{*},v^{*},w^{*})\right\|=0.

Together with Theorem 2.2, this describes accurately the spreading of the faster predator when cu∗>cv∗c_{u}^{*}>c_{v}^{*}. However, it is still only known that vv spreads at least at speed cv∗⁣∗c_{v}^{**}, and at most at speed cv∗c_{v}^{*}. It remains an open question whether vv has a definite spreading speed and what this spreading speed is. While one may expect that the spreading speed of vv is cv∗⁣∗c_{v}^{**}, which indeed corresponds to the linear invasion speed into the intermediate semi-trivial steady state (p~,0,q~)(\tilde{p},0,\tilde{q}), we can actually construct a situation where the spreading speed is strictly faster than cv∗⁣∗c_{v}^{**}. This is comparable to the nonlocally pulled phenomenon which occurs in competition systems [13].

Theorem 2.6 (Nonlocal Pulling).

Under the same assumptions as in Theorem 2.5, assume furthermore that

1−2​a​b−h>0,cv∗⁣∗−(cv∗⁣∗)2−4​d2​r2​(a​β−1−h⁡(a−1))>(cu∗)2−(cv∗)22​(cu∗−cv∗⁣∗).\begin{split}&{1-2ab-h>0,}\\ &c_{v}^{**}-\sqrt{\left(c_{v}^{**}\right)^{2}-4d_{2}r_{2}(a\beta-1-h(a-1))}>\frac{\left(c_{u}^{*}\right)^{2}-\left(c_{v}^{*}\right)^{2}}{2(c_{u}^{*}-c_{v}^{**})}.\end{split}

Then there exists c>cv∗⁣∗c>c_{v}^{**} (independent of the initial data) such that

lim inft→+∞inf|x|≤c​tv⁡(t,x)>0.\liminf_{t\to+\infty}\inf_{|x|\leq ct}v(t,x)>0.
Remark 2.1.

The conditions proposed above hold in particular when 1−2​a​b−h>01-2ab-h>0 and 0<d1​r1−d2​r20<d_{1}r_{1}-d_{2}r_{2} is sufficiently small. This ensures that there is a set of parameters which satisfy the assumptions of Theorem 2.6, thus the nonlocal pulling phenomenon does indeed occur.

3. Preliminaries

3.1. Some a priori estimates

Let (u,v,w)(u,v,w) be a solution of the Cauchy problem for system (1.1)-(1.3) with the initial condition (1.5), under the assumption (1.6). It is clear that the solution (u,v,w)(u,v,w) exists globally. By the (strong) comparison principle (for scalar equations), it is easy to see that u,v,w>0u,v,w>0 in (0,∞)×ℝ(0,\infty)\times\mathbb{R}, and w<1w<1 in (0,∞)×ℝ(0,\infty)\times\mathbb{R}. Then

{ut≤d1​ux​x+r1​u​(a−1−u)+μ⁡(v−u),vt≤d2​ux​x+r2​v​(a−1−v)+μ⁡(u−v).\displaystyle\begin{cases}u_{t}\leq d_{1}u_{xx}+r_{1}u(a-1-u)+\mu(v-u),\\ v_{t}\leq d_{2}u_{xx}+r_{2}v(a-1-v)+\mu(u-v).\end{cases}

This system is of the cooperative type and satisfies a comparison principle. It is then straightforward that u,v<a−1u,v<a-1 in (0,∞)×ℝ(0,\infty)\times\mathbb{R}. Moreover, by (1.6) and (1.3), another comparison principle gives that w≥βw\geq\beta in (0,∞)×ℝ(0,\infty)\times\mathbb{R}.

We sum up the above in the following proposition.

Proposition 3.1.

Assume that (u,v,w)(u,v,w) solves (1.1)-(1.3) together with (1.5) with μ≥0\mu\geq 0, where 0≤u0,v0≤a−10\leq u_{0},v_{0}\leq a-1, β≤w0≤1\beta\leq w_{0}\leq 1. Then the inequalities 0≤u,v≤a−10\leq u,v\leq a-1, β≤w≤1\beta\leq w\leq 1 also hold for all t>0t>0.

3.2. Orbit closure sets and key persistence lemmas

In this section and for convenience, we introduce

(3.1) X0:={(u0,v0,w0)∈(UC0(ℝ;ℝ))3| 0≤u0,v0≤a−1,β≤w0≤1},X_{0}:=\{(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0})\in(UC^{0}(\mathbb{R};\mathbb{R}))^{3}\,|\ 0\leq u_{0},\ v_{0}\leq a-1,\ \beta\leq w_{0}\leq 1\},

where U​C0​(ℝ,ℝ)UC^{0}(\mathbb{R};\mathbb{R}) denotes the set of uniformly continuous and bounded functions from ℝ\mathbb{R} to ℝ\mathbb{R}. In other words, X0X_{0} denotes the set of initial data satisfying (1.6).

According to Proposition 3.1, for any (u0,v0,w0)∈X0(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0})\in X_{0}, the associated solution (u,v,w)(u,v,w) satisfies the same inequalities for all positive times, i.e.,

0≤u,v≤a−1,β≤w≤1.0\leq u,v\leq a-1,\quad\beta\leq w\leq 1.

We also observe the following property. Let (u,v,w)(u,v,w) be a solution of (1.1)-(1.3) with initial data (u0,v0,w0)∈X0(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0})\in X_{0}. If μ>0\mu>0 and there exists (t0,x0)∈ℝ2(t_{0},x_{0})\in\mathbb{R}^{2} with either u⁡(t0,x0)=0u(t_{0},x_{0})=0 or v⁡(t0,x0)=0v(t_{0},x_{0})=0, then, by the strong maximum principle,

u⁡(t,x)=0​ and ​v​(t,x)=0​ for all ​(t,x)∈ℝ2.u(t,x)=0\text{ and }v(t,x)=0\text{ for all }(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}.

On the other hand, if μ=0\mu=0 and there exists (t0,x0)∈ℝ2(t_{0},x_{0})\in\mathbb{R}^{2} with u⁡(t0,x0)=0u(t_{0},x_{0})=0 (resp. v⁡(t0,x0)=0v(t_{0},x_{0})=0), then

u⁡(t,x)=0​(resp. ​v​(t,x)=0)​ for all ​(t,x)∈ℝ2.u(t,x)=0\;\;(\text{resp. }v(t,x)=0)\text{ for all }(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}.

In order to state our key lemma, it is also convenient to introduce some new function set ω0​(c2,c1)\omega_{0}(c_{2},c_{1}), which roughly stands for the closure (with respect to the locally uniform topology) of the orbits of the solution in moving frames with speeds in the interval [c2,c1][c_{2},c_{1}]. More precisely:

Definition 3.1.

For any (u0,v0,w0)∈X0(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0})\in X_{0}, and any 0≤c2<c10\leq c_{2}<c_{1}, we define the set

ω0(c2,c1):=closure{(u,v,w)(t,⋅+ct)|t≥0,c∈[c2,c1]}⊂X0,\omega_{0}\left(c_{2},c_{1}\right):=closure\,\{(u,v,w)(t,\cdot+ct)\,|\ t\geq 0,\ c\in[c_{2},c_{1}]\}\subset X_{0},

where (u,v,w)(u,v,w) denotes the solution of (1.1)-(1.3) with the initial data (u0,v0,w0)(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0}). Herein the closure is understood with respect to the locally uniform topology in ℝ\mathbb{R}.

We point out that the fact that ω0​(c2,c1)\omega_{0}(c_{2},c_{1}) is a subset of X0X_{0} is a straightforward consequence of the above discussion together with standard parabolic estimates. In the sequel we have to keep in mind that this set depends on the initial data and, for notational convenience we omit to explicitly write down the dependence with respect to the initial data.

We now turn to some important lemma that shall be used several times throughout this manuscript.

Corollary 3.3.

Remark 3.1.

The same results as in Lemma 3.2 and Corollary 3.3 also hold for negative speeds with straightforward adaptations.

3.3. Some eigenvalue problems

We conclude this section by a computational lemma that shall be used in the sequel in particular to check the assumptions of Lemma 3.2 and Corollary 3.3.

Lemma 3.4.

Let d>0d>0, c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}, a∈ℝa\in\mathbb{R} and R>0R>0 be given. Then the principal eigenvalue λR\lambda_{R} of the following Dirichlet elliptic problem

{−dφ′′(x)−cφ′(x)+aφ(x)=λRφ(x), for x∈(−R,R),φ⁡(±R)=0​ and ​φ>0​ on ​(−R,R),\begin{cases}-d\varphi^{\prime\prime}(x)-c\varphi^{\prime}(x)+a\varphi(x)=\lambda_{R}\varphi(x),\;\mbox{ for }x\in(-R,R),\vskip 3.0pt\\ \varphi(\pm R)=0\text{ and }\varphi>0\text{ on }(-R,R),\end{cases}

is given by

λR=a+c24​d+d​π24​R2.\lambda_{R}=a+\frac{c^{2}}{4d}+\frac{d\pi^{2}}{4R^{2}}.

This is classical and we omit the proof.

In the ‘two mutants’ case, we need an analogous result for a (cooperative) system as follows.

Proposition 3.5.

Let μ>0\mu>0, c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}, δ≥0\delta\geq 0 and R>0R>0 be given. Consider the following principal eigenvalue problem:

{−d1φx​x−cφx−r1φ(a−1−2δ)−μ(ψ−φ)=ΛRφ, for x∈(−R,R),−d2ψx​x−cψx−r2ψ(a−1−2r1r2δ)−μ(φ−ψ)=ΛRψ, for x∈(−R,R),φ(±R)=ψ(±R)=0 and φ,ψ>0 on (−R,R).\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}-d_{1}\varphi_{xx}-c\varphi_{x}-r_{1}\varphi(a-1-2\delta)-\mu(\psi-\varphi)=\Lambda_{R}\varphi,\ \ \mbox{ for }x\in(-R,R),\\ -d_{2}\psi_{xx}-c\psi_{x}-r_{2}\psi(a-1-2\frac{r_{1}}{r_{2}}\delta)-\mu(\varphi-\psi)=\Lambda_{R}\psi,\ \ \mbox{ for }x\in(-R,R),\\ \varphi(\pm R)=\psi(\pm R)=0\text{ and }\varphi,\psi>0\text{ on }(-R,R).\end{array}\right.

Then there exists a unique ΛR​(c,δ)\Lambda_{R}(c,\delta) such that this eigenvalue problem admits an eigenfunction pair (φ,ψ)(\varphi,\psi) with φ,ψ>0\varphi,\psi>0 in (−R,R)(-R,R). It satisfies ΛR​(c,δ)=ΛR​(c,0)+2​r1​δ\Lambda_{R}(c,\delta)=\Lambda_{R}(c,0)+2r_{1}\delta and ΛR​(−c,0)=ΛR​(c,0)\Lambda_{R}(-c,0)=\Lambda_{R}(c,0). Moreover, for each |c|<cμ∗|c|<c^{*}_{\mu}, there exist δ0>0\delta_{0}>0 and R0R_{0} such that

ΛR​(c,δ)<0,∀δ∈[0,δ0],∀R≥R0.\Lambda_{R}(c,\delta)<0,\;\forall\delta\in[0,\delta_{0}],\;\forall R\geq R_{0}.

Since this result was proved in [12], we only give a brief sketch of the argument.

Proof.

First, by the classical Krein-Rutman theory, there exists a unique ΛR​(c,δ)\Lambda_{R}(c,\delta) such that this eigenvalue problem admits a positive eigenfunction pair. The symmetry with respect to cc follows from the uniqueness of this eigenvalue and by changing xx to −x-x into the system.

We consider now 0≤c<cμ∗0\leq c<c^{*}_{\mu}. As R→+∞R\to+\infty, ΛR​(c,δ)\Lambda_{R}(c,\delta) converges to a generalized principal eigenvalue of the operator

𝐀⁡[φ,ψ]:=(−d1​φx​x−c​φx−r1​φ​(a−1−2​δ)−μ⁡(ψ−φ)−d2​ψx​x−c​ψx−r2​ψ​(a−1−2​r1r2​δ)−μ⁡(φ−ψ));\mathbf{A}[\varphi,\psi]:=\left(\begin{array}[]{l}-d_{1}\varphi_{xx}-c\varphi_{x}-r_{1}\varphi(a-1-2\delta)-\mu(\psi-\varphi)\\ -d_{2}\psi_{xx}-c\psi_{x}-r_{2}\psi(a-1-2\frac{r_{1}}{r_{2}}\delta)-\mu(\varphi-\psi)\end{array}\right);

see [12, Theorem 4.2]. More precisely, this generalized principal eigenvalue is defined as

sup{λ∈ℝ|∃(φ,ψ)∈C2(ℝ,ℝ+∗×ℝ+∗),𝐀[φ,ψ]≥λ[φ,ψ]},\sup\,\{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\,|\ \exists(\varphi,\psi)\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}_{+}^{*}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}^{*}),\quad\mathbf{A}[\varphi,\psi]\geq\lambda[\varphi,\psi]\},

where the inequality is to be understood componentwise. It also turns out (see [12, Lemma 6.4]) that this generalized principal eigenvalue coincides with the maximum of the function

γ∈[0,+∞)↦−Λ[μ,γ]+2r1δ+cγ,\gamma\in[0,+\infty)\mapsto-\Lambda[\mu,\gamma]+2r_{1}\delta+c\gamma,

where Λ⁡[μ,γ]\Lambda[\mu,\gamma] is the Perron-Frobenius eigenvalue of the matrix defined by (2.3). In other words, one has uniformly with respect to δ\delta that

limR→+∞ΛR​(c,δ)=maxγ≥0⁡{−Λ⁡[μ,γ]+c​γ}+2​r1​δ.\lim_{R\to+\infty}\Lambda_{R}(c,\delta)=\max_{\gamma\geq 0}\left\{-\Lambda[\mu,\gamma]+c\gamma\right\}+2r_{1}\delta.

Recalling that Λ⁡[μ,0]>0\Lambda[\mu,0]>0,

cμ∗:=minγ>0⁡Λ⁡[μ,γ]γ>0,c_{\mu}^{*}:=\min_{\gamma>0}\frac{\Lambda[\mu,\gamma]}{\gamma}>0,

and 0≤c<cμ∗0\leq c<c^{*}_{\mu}, one gets the existence of R0>0R_{0}>0 large enough and δ0>0\delta_{0}>0 small enough such that for all R≥R0R\geq R_{0} and δ∈[0,δ0]\delta\in[0,\delta_{0}] one has

ΛR​(c,δ)<0.\Lambda_{R}(c,\delta)<0.

The proposition is proved. ∎

We point out that it follows from this proposition that solutions of the sub-system

{ut=d1​ux​x+r1​u​(a−1−u−k​v)+μ⁡(v−u),vt=d2​vx​x+r2​v​(a−1−h​u−v)+μ⁡(u−v),\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}u_{t}=d_{1}u_{xx}+r_{1}u(a-1-u-kv)+\mu(v-u),\\ v_{t}=d_{2}v_{xx}+r_{2}v(a-1-hu-v)+\mu(u-v),\end{array}\right.

which arises from taking w≡1w\equiv 1 in (1.1)-(1.2), spread with speed cμ∗c^{*}_{\mu} when 0<μ≤(a−1)​min⁡{r1,r2}/20<\mu\leq(a-1)\min\{r_{1},r_{2}\}/2. We refer to Girardin [12] for a proof of this result, in a more general framework including an arbitrary number of mutants. This relies on the fact that this sub-system roughly has a cooperative structure around the trivial steady state (0,0)(0,0), i.e., the linearized system around (0,0)(0,0) is cooperative, since competitive terms are nonlinear. As a matter of fact, we believe that our analysis for the predator-prey system could also work when we increase the number of mutants. As we shall see later, our proof relies on a similar construction of subsolutions as in [12], hence on the above proposition.

4. Uniformly positive entire solutions

In this section, we state some Liouville type results on the stationary solutions of both the full ‘two competitors’ system and its sub-systems with only one predator. This relies on a Lyapunov approach and it shall allow us to describe the shape of the solutions behind the propagation fronts. Throughout this section we shall assume that

μ=0.\mu=0.

4.1. Two-dimensional sub-systems

We start with an important lemma on bounded and uniformly positive entire solutions of the sub-system

{ut−d1​ux​x=u​F​(u,0,w),wt−d3​wx​x=w​H​(u,0,w),​t∈ℝ,x∈ℝ.\begin{cases}u_{t}-d_{1}u_{xx}=uF(u,0,w),\\ w_{t}-d_{3}w_{xx}=wH(u,0,w),\end{cases}t\in\mathbb{R},\;x\in\mathbb{R}.

Our result reads as follows.

Lemma 4.1.

Let (u,w)=(u,w)​(t,x)(u,w)=(u,w)(t,x) be an entire solution of the above system such that there exist constants M>m>0M>m>0 with

m≤u⁡(t,x)≤M,m≤w⁡(t,x)≤M,∀(t,x)∈ℝ2.m\leq u(t,x)\leq M,\;m\leq w(t,x)\leq M,\;\forall(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}.

Then (u,w)≡(p~,q~)(u,w)\equiv\left(\tilde{p},\tilde{q}\right), where the stationary state (p~,q~)\left(\tilde{p},\tilde{q}\right) is defined in (2.1).

Before we prove this result, we point out that the roles of uu can easily be inverted. In particular, considering

{vt−d2​vx​x=v​G​(0,v,w),wt−d3​wx​x=w​H​(0,v,w),​t∈ℝ,x∈ℝ,\begin{cases}v_{t}-d_{2}v_{xx}=vG(0,v,w),\\ w_{t}-d_{3}w_{xx}=wH(0,v,w),\end{cases}t\in\mathbb{R},\;x\in\mathbb{R},

we also have:

Lemma 4.2.

Let (v,w)=(v,w)​(t,x)(v,w)=(v,w)(t,x) be an entire solution of the above system such that there exist constants M>m>0M>m>0 with

m≤v⁡(t,x)≤M,m≤w⁡(t,x)≤M,∀(t,x)∈ℝ2.m\leq v(t,x)\leq M,\;m\leq w(t,x)\leq M,\;\forall(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}.

Then (v,w)≡(p~,q~)(v,w)\equiv\left(\tilde{p},\tilde{q}\right), where the stationary state (p~,q~)\left(\tilde{p},\tilde{q}\right) is defined in (2.1).

Proof.

Since both results are actually the same up to renaming parameters, we only prove Lemma 4.1. In order to prove this lemma we make use of a Lyapunov like argument, inspired from [4, 7].

Define the function g⁡(x)=x−ln⁡(x)−1g(x)=x-\ln(x)-1. Recalling the definition of (p~,q~)\left(\tilde{p},\tilde{q}\right) in (2.1) one has

F⁡(u,0,w)=r1​[p~−u+a⁡(w−q~)],H⁡(u,0,w)=r2​[b⁡(p~−u)+(q~−w)].F(u,0,w)=r_{1}[\tilde{p}-u+a(w-\tilde{q})],\;\;H(u,0,w)=r_{2}[b(\tilde{p}-u)+(\tilde{q}-w)].

Consider also the function V=V⁡(u,w)V=V(u,w) given by

V⁡(u,w)=b​r2​p~​g​(up~)+a​r1​q~​g​(wq~):=V1​(u)+V2​(w).V(u,w)=br_{2}\tilde{p}g\left(\frac{u}{\tilde{p}}\right)+ar_{1}\tilde{q}g\left(\frac{w}{\tilde{q}}\right):=V_{1}(u)+V_{2}(w).

Note that the Lie Derivative of VV along X=(u​F​(u,0,w),w​H​(u,0,w))X=(uF(u,0,w),wH(u,0,w)), denoted by LX​VL_{X}V, is given by

LX​V​(u,w)=Vu​(u,w)​u​F​(u,0,w)+Vw​(u,w)​w​H​(u,0,w)=b​r1​r2​(u−p~)​[p~−u+a⁡(w−q~)]+a​r1​r2​(w−q~)​[b⁡(p~−u)+(q~−w)]=−b​r1​r2​(u−p~)2−a​r1​r2​(w−q~)2.\begin{split}L_{X}V(u,w)&=V_{u}(u,w)uF(u,0,w)+V_{w}(u,w)wH(u,0,w)\\ &=br_{1}r_{2}\left(u-\tilde{p}\right)[\tilde{p}-u+a(w-\tilde{q})]+ar_{1}r_{2}(w-\tilde{q})[b(\tilde{p}-u)+(\tilde{q}-w)]\\ &=-br_{1}r_{2}\left(u-\tilde{p}\right)^{2}-ar_{1}r_{2}(w-\tilde{q})^{2}.\end{split}

Now observe that there exists some constant α>0\alpha>0 such that

LX​V​(u,w)≤−α​V​(u,w),∀(u,w)∈[m,M]×[m,M].L_{X}V(u,w)\leq-\alpha V(u,w),\;\forall(u,w)\in[m,M]\times[m,M].

Next, consider a function φ\varphi smooth, non-negative and such that

φ⁡(x)={1, if x∈[−1,1],0, if |x|≥2.\varphi(x)=\begin{cases}1,\quad\text{ if $x\in[-1,1]$,}\\ 0,\quad\text{ if $|x|\geq 2$.}\end{cases}

Define for R>0R>0 the functional

ℰR​(t)=∫ℝφ⁡(R−1​x)​V​(u⁡(t,x),w⁡(t,x))​𝑑x.\mathcal{E}_{R}(t)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\varphi(R^{-1}x)V(u(t,x),w(t,x))dx.

Then one has, for all t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R},

dd​t​ℰR​(t)=∫ℝφ⁡(R−1​x)​[V1′​(u)​d1​ux​x+V2′​(w)​d3​wx​x]​𝑑x+∫ℝφ⁡(R−1​x)​LX​V​(u,w)​𝑑x,\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal{E}_{R}(t)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\varphi(R^{-1}x)[V_{1}^{\prime}(u)d_{1}u_{xx}+V_{2}^{\prime}(w)d_{3}w_{xx}]dx+\int_{\mathbb{R}}\varphi(R^{-1}x)L_{X}V(u,w)dx,

so that

dd​t​ℰR​(t)=R−2​∫ℝφ′′​(R−1​x)​d1​V1​(u)​𝑑x−d1​∫ℝφ⁡(R−1​x)​V1′′​(u)​(ux)2​𝑑x+R−2∫ℝφ′′(R−1x)d3V2(u)dx−d3∫ℝφ(R−1x)V2′′(u)(wx)2dx+∫ℝφ(R−1x)LXV(u,w)dx.\begin{split}\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal{E}_{R}(t)=&R^{-2}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\varphi^{\prime\prime}(R^{-1}x)d_{1}V_{1}(u)dx-d_{1}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\varphi(R^{-1}x)V_{1}^{\prime\prime}(u)(u_{x})^{2}dx\\ &+R^{-2}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\varphi^{\prime\prime}(R^{-1}x)d_{3}V_{2}(u)dx-d_{3}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\varphi(R^{-1}x)V_{2}^{\prime\prime}(u)(w_{x})^{2}dx\\ &+\int_{\mathbb{R}}\varphi(R^{-1}x)L_{X}V(u,w)dx.\end{split}

Since V1′′≥0V_{1}^{\prime\prime}\geq 0, V2′′≥0V_{2}^{\prime\prime}\geq 0 and m≤u,v≤Mm\leq u,v\leq M, we obtain that there exists some constant K>0K>0 independent of RR such that

dd​t​ℰR​(t)≤KR−α​ℰR​(t),∀t∈ℝ.\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal{E}_{R}(t)\leq\frac{K}{R}-\alpha\mathcal{E}_{R}(t),\;\forall t\in\mathbb{R}.

This yields

ℰR​(t)≤Kα​R,∀t∈ℝ,∀R>0.\mathcal{E}_{R}(t)\leq\frac{K}{\alpha R},\;\forall t\in\mathbb{R},\;\forall R>0.

This ensures that ℰR​(t)→0\mathcal{E}_{R}(t)\to 0 as R→+∞R\to+\infty uniformly for t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}, and the result follows by applying Fatou’s lemma. ∎

4.2. The full system

Lemma 4.3.

Let (u,v,w)=(u,v,w)​(t,x)(u,v,w)=(u,v,w)(t,x) be a bounded entire solution of (1.1)-(1.3) such that

(4.1) min⁡(inf(t,x)∈ℝ2u⁡(t,x),inf(t,x)∈ℝ2v⁡(t,x),inf(t,x)∈ℝ2w⁡(t,x))>0.\min\left(\inf_{(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}}u(t,x),\inf_{(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}}v(t,x),\inf_{(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}}w(t,x)\right)>0.

Then (u,v,w)≡(u∗,v∗,w∗),(u,v,w)\equiv\left(u^{*},v^{*},w^{*}\right), where the stationary state (u∗,v∗,w∗)(u^{*},v^{*},w^{*}) is defined in (2.2).

Proof.

The proof of this lemma makes use of similar arguments as the ones used for Lemma 4.1. Let (u,v,w)(u,v,w) be a bounded entire solution of (1.1)-(1.3) satisfying (4.1). We denote by 0<m≤M0<m\leq M the lower and upper bounds of (u,v,w)(u,v,w). Recall that we defined the function g⁡(x)=x−ln⁡(x)−1g(x)=x-\ln(x)-1, and let us consider the function Φ=Φ⁡(u,v,w)\Phi=\Phi(u,v,w) given by

Φ⁡(u,v,w):=u∗​g​(uu∗)+r1​v∗r2​g​(vv∗)+r1​a​w∗r3​b​g​(ww∗).\Phi(u,v,w):=u^{*}g\left(\frac{u}{u^{*}}\right)+\frac{r_{1}v^{*}}{r_{2}}g\left(\frac{v}{v^{*}}\right)+\frac{r_{1}aw^{*}}{r_{3}b}g\left(\frac{w}{w^{*}}\right).

Let us compute the Lie derivative of Φ\Phi, denoted by LX​ΦL_{X}\Phi, along the three dimensional vector field X=(u​F​(u,v,w),v​G​(u,v,w),w​H​(u,v,w))X=(uF(u,v,w),vG(u,v,w),wH(u,v,w)) associated to the kinetic part of (1.1)-(1.3). It reads for each u>0u>0, v>0v>0 and w>0w>0 as:

LX​Φ​(u,v,w)\displaystyle L_{X}\Phi(u,v,w)
=r1​{−(u−u∗)2−k⁡(u−u∗)​(v−v∗)+a⁡(u−u∗)​(w−w∗)}\displaystyle=r_{1}\{-(u-u^{*})^{2}-k(u-u^{*})(v-v^{*})+a(u-u^{*})(w-w^{*})\}
+r1​{−h⁡(u−u∗)​(v−v∗)−(v−v∗)2+a⁡(v−v∗)​(w−w∗)}\displaystyle\qquad+r_{1}\{-h(u-u^{*})(v-v^{*})-(v-v^{*})^{2}+a(v-v^{*})(w-w^{*})\}
+r1​ab​{−b⁡(u−u∗)​(w−w∗)−b⁡(v−v∗)​(w−w∗)−(w−w∗)2}\displaystyle\qquad+\frac{r_{1}a}{b}\{-b(u-u^{*})(w-w^{*})-b(v-v^{*})(w-w^{*})-(w-w^{*})^{2}\}
=−r1​(u−u∗)2−r1​(k+h)​(u−u∗)​(v−v∗)−r1​(v−v∗)2−r1​ab​(w−w∗)2.\displaystyle=-r_{1}(u-u^{*})^{2}-r_{1}(k+h)(u-u^{*})(v-v^{*})-r_{1}(v-v^{*})^{2}-\frac{r_{1}a}{b}(w-w^{*})^{2}.

Now observe that for all (X1,X2)=(r​cos⁡θ,r​sin⁡θ)∈ℝ2(X_{1},X_{2})=(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\in\mathbb{R}^{2} one has

X12+(k+h)​X1​X2+X22=r2​(1+(h+k)​cos⁡θ​sin⁡θ)=r2​[1+h+k2​sin⁡(2​θ)]≥r2​[1−h+k2]=[1−h+k2]​(X12+X22).\begin{split}&X_{1}^{2}+(k+h)X_{1}X_{2}+X_{2}^{2}=r^{2}(1+(h+k)\cos\theta\sin\theta)\\ &=r^{2}\left[1+\frac{h+k}{2}\sin(2\theta)\right]\geq r^{2}\left[1-\frac{h+k}{2}\right]=\left[1-\frac{h+k}{2}\right](X_{1}^{2}+X_{2}^{2}).\end{split}

As a consequence, since 0<h,k<10<h,k<1 (see (1.4)) one has 0<h+k<20<h+k<2 and there exists α>0\alpha>0 such that for all u>0u>0, v>0v>0 and w>0w>0 one has

LX​Φ​(u,v,w)≤−α⁡[(u−u∗)2+(v−v∗)2+(w−w∗)2].L_{X}\Phi(u,v,w)\leq-\alpha\left[(u-u^{*})^{2}+(v-v^{*})^{2}+(w-w^{*})^{2}\right].

Furthermore, recalling the definition of Φ\Phi above, there exists β>0\beta>0 such that

LX​Φ​(u,v,w)≤−β​Φ​(u,v,w),∀(u,v,w)∈[m,M]3.L_{X}\Phi(u,v,w)\leq-\beta\Phi(u,v,w),\;\forall(u,v,w)\in[m,M]^{3}.

From this inequality, the proof of Lemma 4.3 follows from the same arguments as the ones used for Lemma 4.1. ∎

5. Proofs of Theorem 2.1 and Theorem 2.2

In this section, we mostly deal with the ‘two mutants’ case, i.e., Theorem 2.1. However, because the arguments for the upper bound on the speeds is very similar, we also include the proof of Theorem 2.2.

5.1. Upper bounds on the spreading speeds

In this subsection we derive upper estimates for the spreading speed of the solution of system (1.1)-(1.3). Our first result is given below. It proves both part (i) of Theorem 2.1 and Theorem 2.2.

Theorem 5.1.

Let (u0,v0,w0)∈X0(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0})\in X_{0} (recall (3.1)) be such that u0u_{0} and v0v_{0} are both nontrivial and compactly supported, and (u,v,w)(u,v,w) be the corresponding solution.

  • (i)

    If μ=0\mu=0, then

    (5.1) limt→+∞sup|x|≥c​tu⁡(t,x)=0,\lim_{t\to+\infty}\sup_{|x|\geq ct}u(t,x)=0,

    for any c>cu∗c>c_{u}^{*}, and

    (5.2) limt→+∞sup|x|≥c​tv⁡(t,x)=0,\lim_{t\to+\infty}\sup_{|x|\geq ct}v(t,x)=0,

    for any c>cv∗c>c_{v}^{*}; moreover,

    (5.3) limt→+∞sup|x|≥c​t|w⁡(t,x)−1|=0,\lim_{t\to+\infty}\sup_{|x|\geq ct}|w(t,x)-1|=0,

    for any c>max⁡{cu∗,cv∗}c>\max\{c_{u}^{*},c_{v}^{*}\}.

  • (ii)

    If μ>0\mu>0, then

    (5.4) limt→+∞sup|x|≥c​tu⁡(t,x)=0,\displaystyle\lim_{t\to+\infty}\sup_{|x|\geq ct}u(t,x)=0,
    (5.5) limt→+∞sup|x|≥c​tv⁡(t,x)=0,\displaystyle\lim_{t\to+\infty}\sup_{|x|\geq ct}v(t,x)=0,
    (5.6) limt→+∞sup|x|≥c​t|w⁡(t,x)−1|=0,\displaystyle\lim_{t\to+\infty}\sup_{|x|\geq ct}|w(t,x)-1|=0,

    for any c>cμ∗c>c_{\mu}^{*}.

Notice that in the case when μ>0\mu>0, then one can assume without loss of generality and as in Theorem 2.1 that the pair (u0,v0)(u_{0},v_{0}) is nontrivial. This immediately comes from the fact that both components must be simultaneously positive or simultaneously identical to 0 for all positive times.

Proof.

First, due to w≤1w\leq 1 and u,v≥0u,v\geq 0 we have that

{ut≤d1​ux​x+r1​u​(a−1−u)+μ⁡(v−u),vt≤d2​vx​x+r2​v​(a−1−v)+μ⁡(u−v),\displaystyle\begin{cases}u_{t}\leq d_{1}u_{xx}+r_{1}u(a-1-u)+\mu(v-u),\\ v_{t}\leq d_{2}v_{xx}+r_{2}v(a-1-v)+\mu(u-v),\end{cases}

for all t>0t>0 and x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}. In the case when μ=0\mu=0, this system is actually uncoupled so that (5.1) and (5.2) follow from a comparison principle and the classical result of [1] for the scalar equation.

In the case when μ>0\mu>0, we further notice that u,vu,v is a subsolution of the following linear system,

{ut≤d1​ux​x+r1​u​(a−1)+μ⁡(v−u),vt≤d2​vx​x+r2​v​(a−1)+μ⁡(u−v),\displaystyle\begin{cases}u_{t}\leq d_{1}u_{xx}+r_{1}u(a-1)+\mu(v-u),\\ v_{t}\leq d_{2}v_{xx}+r_{2}v(a-1)+\mu(u-v),\end{cases}

which satisfies a comparison principle. Recalling the definition of cμ∗c_{\mu}^{*} in (2.4), this linear system admits a solution of the type

(p,q)​e−γ⁡(x−cμ∗​t),(p,q)e^{-\gamma(x-c_{\mu}^{*}t)},

where pp, qq and γ\gamma are positive. By applying the comparison principle, we obtain (5.4) and (5.5).

Let us now deal with ww, i.e., (5.3) and (5.6). The argument is the same in both cases. Proceed by contradiction and assume that there exists some c>max⁡{cu∗,cv∗}c>\max\{c_{u}^{*},c_{v}^{*}\} (if μ=0\mu=0) or c>cμ∗c>c_{\mu}^{*} (if μ>0\mu>0), and a sequence {(tn,xn)}\{(t_{n},x_{n})\} such that tn→+∞t_{n}\to+\infty, |xn|≥c​tn|x_{n}|\geq ct_{n} and

lim supn→+∞w⁡(tn,xn)<1.\limsup_{n\to+\infty}w(t_{n},x_{n})<1.

Thanks to standard parabolic estimates (recall that all three components are uniformly bounded by Proposition 3.1), we can assume up to extraction of a sub-sequence that (u,v,w)​(t+tn,x+xn)(u,v,w)(t+t_{n},x+x_{n}) converges to an entire in time solution (u∞,v∞,w∞)(u_{\infty},v_{\infty},w_{\infty}) of the same system. From what we have proved above, we know that u∞≡v∞≡0u_{\infty}\equiv v_{\infty}\equiv 0, and thus w∞w_{\infty} solves

(w∞)t=d3​(w∞)x​x+r3​w∞​(1−w∞).(w_{\infty})_{t}=d_{3}(w_{\infty})_{xx}+r_{3}w_{\infty}(1-w_{\infty}).

Recalling that ww, hence w∞w_{\infty}, is everywhere larger than β\beta, we conclude that w∞≡1w_{\infty}\equiv 1. This is a contradiction and completes the proof. ∎

5.2. Spreading for the two mutants system: the case when μ>0\mu>0

In this subsection, we assume that 0<μ≤(a−1)​min⁡{r1,r2}/20<\mu\leq(a-1)\min\{r_{1},r_{2}\}/2, so that uu and vv denote the densities of two mutant types of the same predator species. As we mentioned before, due to μ>0\mu>0, the sub-system composed of equations (1.1)-(1.2) with constant ww roughly has a cooperative structure around the trivial steady state (0,0)(0,0).

To prove the second part of Theorem 2.1, we apply Lemma 3.2 and more precisely its Corollary 3.3 with c1=cμ∗c_{1}=c_{\mu}^{*}. According to this aforementioned result, part (ii) of Theorem 2.1 directly follows from the next lemma, which shows that uu and vv cannot go extinct simultaneously in a moving frame with speed less than cμ∗c^{*}_{\mu}.

Lemma 5.2.

For any c∈[0,cμ∗)c\in[0,c^{*}_{\mu}), there exists some ε⁡(c)>0\varepsilon(c)>0 such that, for any initial data satisfying u0+v0≢0u_{0}+v_{0}\not\equiv 0, 0≤u0,v0≤a−10\leq u_{0},v_{0}\leq a-1 and β≤w0≤1\beta\leq w_{0}\leq 1, the corresponding solution (u,v,w)(u,v,w) satisfies

lim supt→+∞(u⁡(t,c​t)+v⁡(t,c​t))≥ε⁡(c).\limsup_{t\to+\infty}\,(u(t,ct)+v(t,ct))\geq\varepsilon(c).
Proof.

First notice that, because μ>0\mu>0, and even if one of the two functions u0u_{0} and v0v_{0} is identically equal to 0, the strong maximum principle ensures that both u>0u>0 and v>0v>0 for positive times.

Let c∈[0,cμ∗)c\in[0,c^{*}_{\mu}) and assume by contradiction that there is a sequence of solutions {(un,vn,wn)}\{(u_{n},v_{n},w_{n})\} with initial data {(u0,n,v0,n,w0,n)}\{(u_{0,n},v_{0,n},w_{0,n})\} such that

(5.7) lim supt→+∞(un​(t,c​t)+vn​(t,c​t))≤1n.\limsup_{t\to+\infty}\,(u_{n}(t,ct)+v_{n}(t,ct))\leq\frac{1}{n}.

This clearly implies that there exists tnt_{n} large enough such that

max⁡{un​(t,c​t),vn​(t,c​t)}≤2n,∀t≥tn.\max\,\{u_{n}(t,ct),v_{n}(t,ct)\}\leq\frac{2}{n},\ \forall t\geq t_{n}.

In particular, passing to the limit as n→+∞n\to+\infty, and applying a strong maximum principle, one may check that for any R>0R>0,

lim supn→+∞supt≥tn,|x−c​t|≤R(un​(t,x)+vn​(t,x))=0.\limsup_{n\to+\infty}\sup_{t\geq t_{n},|x-ct|\leq R}(u_{n}(t,x)+v_{n}(t,x))=0.

We next claim that, for any R>0R>0,

(5.8) lim supn→+∞supt≥tn,|x−c​t|≤R|wn​(t,x)−1|=0.\limsup_{n\to+\infty}\sup_{t\geq t_{n},|x-ct|\leq R}|w_{n}(t,x)-1|=0.

Proceed by contradiction and take a sequence {(sn,xn)}\{(s_{n},x_{n})\} with sn≥tns_{n}\geq t_{n} and xn∈(c​sn−R,c​sn+R)x_{n}\in(cs_{n}-R,cs_{n}+R) such that lim supn→+∞wn​(sn,xn)<1\limsup_{n\to+\infty}w_{n}(s_{n},x_{n})<1. Since solutions are bounded uniformly with respect to nn, we can use standard parabolic estimates and extract a sub-sequence so that (un,vn,wn)​(t+sn,x+xn)(u_{n},v_{n},w_{n})(t+s_{n},x+x_{n}) converges to an entire in time solution (u∞,v∞,w∞)(u_{\infty},v_{\infty},w_{\infty}). By construction, u∞,v∞≥0u_{\infty},v_{\infty}\geq 0 and u∞​(t,0)=v∞​(t,0)=0u_{\infty}(t,0)=v_{\infty}(t,0)=0 for all t>0t>0. Hence, by the strong comparison principle, we have that u∞≡v∞≡0u_{\infty}\equiv v_{\infty}\equiv 0. Thus w∞w_{\infty} satisfies

(w∞)t=d3​(w∞)x​x+r3​w∞​(1−w∞).(w_{\infty})_{t}=d_{3}(w_{\infty})_{xx}+r_{3}w_{\infty}(1-w_{\infty}).

Since w∞≥βw_{\infty}\geq\beta, we deduce that w∞≡1w_{\infty}\equiv 1, which contradicts the fact that w∞​(0,0)<1w_{\infty}(0,0)<1. The claim (5.8) is thus proved.

Then, for any small δ>0\delta>0 and large R>0R>0, one can increase nn so that (un,vn)(u_{n},v_{n}) satisfies

{(un)t≥d1​(un)x​x+r1​un​(a−1−2​δ)+μ⁡(vn−un),(vn)t≥d2​(vn)x​x+r2​vn​(a−1−2​r1r2​δ)+μ⁡(un−vn),\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}(u_{n})_{t}\geq d_{1}(u_{n})_{xx}+r_{1}u_{n}(a-1-2\delta)+\mu(v_{n}-u_{n}),\\ (v_{n})_{t}\geq d_{2}(v_{n})_{xx}+r_{2}v_{n}(a-1-2\frac{r_{1}}{r_{2}}\delta)+\mu(u_{n}-v_{n}),\end{array}\right.

for t≥tnt\geq t_{n} and |x−c​tn|≤R|x-ct_{n}|\leq R. Notice that this is a cooperative system, hence it satisfies the comparison principle. In particular, we get that

un​(t,x+c​t)≥u¯n​(t,x),vn​(t,x+c​t)≥v¯n​(t,x),u_{n}(t,x+ct)\geq\underline{u}_{n}(t,x)\,,\quad v_{n}(t,x+ct)\geq\underline{v}_{n}(t,x),

for all t≥tnt\geq t_{n} and |x|≤R|x|\leq R, where

(u¯n,v¯n)​(t,x):=ϵ​e−ΛR​t​(φ,ψ)​(x),(\underline{u}_{n},\underline{v}_{n})(t,x):=\epsilon e^{-\Lambda_{R}t}(\varphi,\psi)(x),

with ΛR\Lambda_{R}, (φ,ψ)(\varphi,\psi) the principal eigenvalue and the associated positive eigenfunction pair from Proposition 3.5, and ϵ>0\epsilon>0 is small enough (possibly depending on nn) so that

un​(tn,x+c​tn)≥ϵ​e−ΛR​tn​φ​(x),vn​(tn,x+c​tn)≥ϵ​e−ΛR​tn​ψ​(x),u_{n}(t_{n},x+ct_{n})\geq\epsilon e^{-\Lambda_{R}t_{n}}\varphi(x)\,,\quad v_{n}(t_{n},x+ct_{n})\geq\epsilon e^{-\Lambda_{R}t_{n}}\psi(x),

for all |x|≤R|x|\leq R. Using again Proposition 3.5, we have that ΛR<0\Lambda_{R}<0 if δ\delta is small enough and RR is large. Thus, un​(t,c​t)≥u¯n​(t,c​t)→+∞u_{n}(t,ct)\geq\underline{u}_{n}(t,ct)\to+\infty as t→+∞t\to+\infty, which contradicts (5.7). The lemma is proved. ∎

Recall here that the above lemma completes the proof of part (ii) of Theorem 2.1, by applying Corollary 3.3 and a symmetry argument to deal with the negative part of the spatial domain. Together with Theorem 5.1, this ends the proof of Theorem 2.1.

6. Lower bounds on the speeds in the competitor case

In this section we derive preliminary lower spreading estimates for the two competitors system, namely when μ=0\mu=0. More precisely, we prove parts (i) and (ii) of Theorem 2.3 in the case when cu∗=cv∗c_{u}^{*}=c_{v}^{*}. However, the results proved in this section can also be applied in the case when cv∗<cu∗c_{v}^{*}<c_{u}^{*} and they shall serve as a starting point in the proofs of Theorem 2.4 in Section 8.

Throughout this section we assume that μ=0\mu=0 and

In particular, we have that 0≤u0,v0≤a−10\leq u_{0},v_{0}\leq a-1 and β≤w0≤1\beta\leq w_{0}\leq 1. We denote by (u,v,w)(u,v,w) the corresponding solution. Then our first result describes a lower spreading estimate for the sum u+vu+v.

Proposition 6.1.

lim supt→+∞(u~n​(t,c​t)+v~n​(t,c​t))≤1n,∀n≥1.\limsup_{t\to+\infty}\left(\tilde{u}_{n}(t,ct)+\tilde{v}_{n}(t,ct)\right)\leq\frac{1}{n},\;\forall n\geq 1.

This in particular means that for each n≥1n\geq 1 there exists tnt_{n} such that

(u~n+v~n)​(t+tn,c⁡(t+tn))≤2n,∀n≥1,∀t≥0.\left(\tilde{u}_{n}+\tilde{v}_{n}\right)(t+t_{n},c(t+t_{n}))\leq\frac{2}{n},\;\forall n\geq 1,\;\forall t\geq 0.

From the above inequality coupled with the strong maximum principle, we have possibly up to a sub-sequence that

uniformly for t≥0t\geq 0 and locally uniformly for x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}.

r1​(a−1−δ)−c24​d1>0,r2​(a−1−δ)−c24​d2>0,\begin{split}&r_{1}(a-1-\delta)-\frac{c^{2}}{4d_{1}}>0,\\ &r_{2}(a-1-\delta)-\frac{c^{2}}{4d_{2}}>0,\end{split}

and, due to Lemma 3.4, choose R>0R>0 large enough such that the principal eigenvalue problems,

satisfy λRi<0\lambda_{R}^{i}<0 for i=1,2i=1,2.

From the above proposition we shall now derive some new estimates for each component uu and vv.

Proposition 6.2.

while (6.5) together with the strong maximum principle imply that v∞​(t,x)≡0v_{\infty}(t,x)\equiv 0.

Furthermore, as an additional corollary of Proposition 6.2 coupled with Lemmas 4.1 and 4.3, we also obtain the following important result which shall be crucially used in the next sections.

Corollary 6.4.

Let (u0,v0,w0)∈X0(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0})\in X_{0} be given and (u,v,w)(u,v,w) be the corresponding solution of (1.1)-(1.3).

  • (i)

    If u0≢0u_{0}\not\equiv 0 and v0≡0v_{0}\equiv 0 then

    limt→+∞(u,v,w)​(t,x)=(p~,0,q~)​ locally uniformly for x∈ℝ.\lim_{t\to+\infty}(u,v,w)(t,x)=(\tilde{p},0,\tilde{q})\text{ locally uniformly for $x\in\mathbb{R}$}.

8. Two competitors: the case when cu∗>cv∗c_{u}^{*}>c_{v}^{*}

In this section, we consider the ‘two competitors’ case, i.e., μ=0\mu=0 and we aim at proving Theorems 2.5 and 2.6. We assume throughout this section that cu∗>cv∗c_{u}^{*}>c_{v}^{*}, so that an intermediate zone may appear where the predator uu invades ahead of the predator vv.

8.1. Spreading of the faster predator

This subsection is concerned with the proof of Theorem 2.5. The main step here is the following proposition, which together with results from previous sections shall immediately imply Theorem 2.5.

8.2. Counter-example: nonlocal pulling

The remaining question is the spreading speed of vv. From Theorem 2.5 and (2.6), we might wonder whether it is cv∗⁣∗c_{v}^{**}. However, it is known that a ‘nonlocal pulling’ phenomenon may occur in competition systems. ‘Nonlocal pulling’ here refers to the fact that the zone ahead of the point cu∗​tc_{u}^{*}t, where uu is close to 0, may have an effect on the speed of its competitor vv. This may be surprising because cu∗c_{u}^{*} is strictly larger than cv∗c_{v}^{*}, thus strictly larger than the spreading speed of vv. We refer to [13] for an example of such a situation in the two species competition system.

Now, we give a short proof that the spreading speed of vv may indeed be strictly larger than cv∗⁣∗c_{v}^{**} in our context of a predator-prey system with two predators. We start by constructing a subsolution for the vv-equation, moving at a speed larger than cv∗⁣∗c_{v}^{**}. In what follows, we let ε>0\varepsilon>0 be arbitrarily small.

Due to Theorem 2.2 and Proposition 3.1, we can assume up to some shift in time that

w⁡(t,x)≥w¯​(t,x),u⁡(t,x)≤u¯​(t,x),w(t,x)\geq\underline{w}(t,x),\quad u(t,x)\leq\overline{u}(t,x),

where

w¯​(t,x):={β if ​x<(cu∗+ε)​t,1−εa if ​x≥(cu∗+ε)​t,\displaystyle\underline{w}(t,x):=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\beta&\mbox{ if }x<(c_{u}^{*}+\varepsilon)t,\\ \displaystyle 1-\frac{\varepsilon}{a}&\mbox{ if }x\geq(c_{u}^{*}+\varepsilon)t,\end{array}\right.
u¯​(t,x):={a−1 if ​x<(cu∗+ε)​t,εh if ​x≥(cu∗+ε)​t.\displaystyle\overline{u}(t,x):=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}a-1&\mbox{ if }x<(c_{u}^{*}+\varepsilon)t,\\ \displaystyle\frac{\varepsilon}{h}&\mbox{ if }x\geq(c_{u}^{*}+\varepsilon)t.\end{array}\right.

Then vv satisfies

vt≥d2​vx​x+r2​v​(−1−h​u¯−v+a​w¯).v_{t}\geq d_{2}v_{xx}+r_{2}v(-1-h\overline{u}-v+a\underline{w}).

vt=d2​vx​x+r2​v​(−1−h​u¯−ε+a​w¯).v_{t}=d_{2}v_{xx}+r_{2}v(-1-h\overline{u}-\varepsilon+a\underline{w}).

If we find such a (bounded) subsolution, then it is a subsolution of the previous nonlinear equation up to multiplying by a small enough constant. Because of the discontinuity at x=(cu∗+ε)​tx=(c_{u}^{*}+\varepsilon)t, we shall ‘glue’ two ansatzes. For ease of notation, let us denote cε:=cu∗+εc_{\varepsilon}:=c_{u}^{*}+\varepsilon.

Let us first deal with the ansatz in the moving frame with speed cεc_{\varepsilon}. We look for a solution of the above linear equation of the type

v1¯​(t,x+cε​t):=e−r​t​e−ν​x​sin⁡(ω​x),\underline{v_{1}}(t,x+c_{\varepsilon}t):=e^{-rt}e^{-\nu x}\sin(\omega x),

whose support is (0,π/ω)(0,\pi/\omega), for some constants rr, ν\nu and ω\omega. In particular, it is included in the part where w¯=1−ε/a\underline{w}=1-{\varepsilon}/{a} and u¯=ε/h\overline{u}={\varepsilon}/{h}. Therefore, putting this into the linearized equation, we find that rr, ν\nu and ω\omega satisfy the system

{cε−2​d2​ν=0,−d2​ω2+d2​ν2−cε​ν+r2​(a−1−3​ε)=−r.\displaystyle\begin{cases}c_{\varepsilon}-2d_{2}\nu=0,\\ -d_{2}\omega^{2}+d_{2}\nu^{2}-c_{\varepsilon}\nu+r_{2}(a-1-3\varepsilon)=-r.\end{cases}

ν=cu∗+ε2​d2\nu=\frac{c_{u}^{*}+\varepsilon}{2d_{2}}

and, taking ω\omega very small, say ω=ε\omega=\varepsilon, we find a compactly supported subsolution in the moving frame with speed cεc_{\varepsilon} which converges to 0 exponentially in time at rate

lim inft→+∞v⁡(t,c​t)>0.\liminf_{t\to+\infty}v(t,ct)>0.

Moreover the uniform positivity of vv for |x|≤c​t|x|\leq ct as t→+∞t\to+\infty follows from Corollary 6.4 (for vv), the fact that uu spreads with speed cu∗c_{u}^{*}, and the same argument as the one developed to prove (8.1).

Now to conclude, let us just try to find one situation which is compatible with previous assumptions. To do this, let us simply vary the parameter d1d_{1} (so that properties of the ODE system and condition (8.9) remain unchanged) and consider the case when d1→(d2​r2r1)+d_{1}\to\left(\frac{d_{2}r_{2}}{r_{1}}\right)^{+} so that 0<cu∗−cv∗→00<c_{u}^{*}-c_{v}^{*}\to 0. In that case, the right hand term of (8.11) converges to 00 while the left hand term converges to

[cv∗⁣∗−(cv∗⁣∗)2−4​d2​r2​(a​β−1−h⁡(a−1))]​(cv∗−cv∗⁣∗)>0.\left[c_{v}^{**}-\sqrt{\left(c_{v}^{**}\right)^{2}-4d_{2}r_{2}(a\beta-1-h(a-1))}\right](c_{v}^{*}-c_{v}^{**})>0.

Therefore, under condition (8.9) and if d1>d2​r2/r1d_{1}>{d_{2}r_{2}}/{r_{1}} but close enough, we find that vv spreads strictly faster than cv∗⁣∗c_{v}^{**}.
